title: The Foundry Under the Sounding
subtitle: What the Sounding Becomes

setting.name: Ossary Deep and the Reckoners' Hall at the Year's Turn
setting.description: Ossary Deep is a drowned foundry-city on the floor of the Grey Sounding, sixty fathoms down: casting-pits, moulding halls, cold furnaces and a bell-house with a roof still on it, all of it laid down before the water came up and left more or less intact because nothing down there rots quickly. It is where the first bells of the chain were poured, four hundred years ago, by people whose descendants are the quiet folk. For eleven years someone has been using it again — the old moulds are still true, the casting-pits still hold, and a bell cast at sixty fathoms and brought up wet is a bell that no surface foundry can be blamed for. Above it, at the far end of the campaign, is the Reckoners' Hall at Tallowport on the last day of the year, with every master on the chain who can get there packed into one long stone room to hear the standings read.
setting.atmosphere: Down: cold, blue-black, enormous and quiet, with a scale that makes everything the party has done so far feel small. Bronze tones travelling miles through water. Halls with their roofs on and their doors still hung. Up: a stone room full of wet coats and two hundred people who have all come a long way to hear a book read out, and the specific electricity of an institution about to have to decide something in public for the first time in a century. The scenario moves between those two registers and the ending happens in the second one.

keyLocations.name: The Threshold of Ossary Deep
keyLocations.description: Where the Sharrow's seaward face drops into the Sounding proper, and where the quiet folk keep their count in bronze on the rock. Sixty fathoms below, the city. The party cannot simply swim this and the getting-down is a real problem with several honest solutions.
features: A drop from eleven fathoms to sixty over about a hundred yards of sloping rock
The bronze count on the reef face, now standing at fifteen
A quiet folk waystation: a bell-frame set into the rock, struck to announce arrivals, which the party will be expected to use
encounters: Solving the descent: water breathing, the quiet folk's help, a diving bell built at Tallowport, or a combination
Being formally received, or formally refused, by the quiet folk at the waystation
Ledda, who has to argue for the party in front of her own people and may lose
secrets: The quiet folk have been recasting a bell of their own for two years, in a pit at the far end of the city, and it is not for rescue
The count is fifteen because a lighter went down off the Sharrow eleven days ago and nobody on the surface has reported her missing

keyLocations.name: The Moulding Halls
keyLocations.description: Long stone halls with their roofs intact, floored in old moulding sand that the water has never quite carried away, racked with four hundred years of bell patterns. The heart of the operation and the most beautiful location in the campaign.
features: Racked patterns for every harbour bell on the chain, original, four centuries old, and still true
Casting-pits, three of them, in current use — the sand disturbed, the runners cleared, the work recent
A ledger of recast bells, kept in bronze plate because paper does not last down here: date, source harbour, destination buoy, and a chop
encounters: The bronze ledger, which is the single most important document in the campaign
The Hollow Bell's working party, who are down here on a schedule and are not expecting company
The bell-house, where a bell is being finished right now
secrets: The bronze ledger records ninety-one recast bells over eleven years, and forty of them are still hung and still ringing false somewhere on the chain
The chop on the ledger is the same chop as the shore-office instruction that sent the Fair Increase

keyLocations.name: The Bell-House
keyLocations.description: A domed stone chamber with a working frame in it and a bell hanging in the frame, half-finished. Where the Hollow Bell's master is, and where the campaign's argument is actually had.
features: A bell on the frame, three-quarters finished, cast from the harbour bell of a Beads hamlet called Sallow Nook that has not yet been reported stolen
A working party of eight, four of them contracted men from Ambergrace and four of them not
The master of the Hollow Bell, who is not a pirate and has an extremely good argument
encounters: The confrontation, which can be a conversation, a fight, or both in either order
The choice of what to do with ninety-one recast bells and a bronze ledger
Getting out with the ledger, which somebody will try very hard to prevent
secrets: The master of the Hollow Bell is Reckoner-Emeritus Corvane Ashe, who sat at the Hall for thirty-one years and wrote most of the modern custom of the Sounding herself

Idony Marrach was down here, once, eleven years ago, at the very beginning — and the money she never had went into a fund at Tallowport that has been quietly victualling three Beads hamlets ever since

keyLocations.name: The Reckoners' Hall at the Year's Turn
keyLocations.description: Tallowport on the last day of the year. Two hundred masters, every Reckoner on the chain, the brass case open on the long table, and the standings read out one by one — including WIDOW'S COMPASS, whatever it now stands at. The climax is here, in public, and it is a decision rather than a fight.
features: The Hall in full session for the first time in a year, which is the only forum on the chain with the standing to decide anything
The ledger of callings, open, on the table, in front of everyone
Two hundred masters who have each personally lost something to this and do not yet know it
encounters: The reading of the party's standing, and whatever it now is
The bronze ledger produced in front of the whole chain
The three endings: break it, reform it, or replace it
secrets: Reckoner Avice Holl has spent the year quietly assembling her own list of anomalies and will produce it the moment somebody else goes first
Whatever the party decides here is decided in front of two hundred people who will go home and act on it, and the campaign should end on what they do

synopsis: Everything the party has chased leads down. The Grace Foundry only finishes what comes up wet, and what comes up wet is cast at sixty fathoms in Ossary Deep — the drowned foundry-city where the first bells of the chain were poured, where the four-hundred-year-old moulds are still true, and where a bronze ledger records ninety-one recast bells over eleven years, forty of them still hung and still ringing false. Down there the party meets the master of the Hollow Bell, who turns out to be a Reckoner-Emeritus who wrote most of the modern custom of the Sounding herself, and who has a genuinely good argument about who the compact has always really served. Then they come up, and the year turns, and the whole chain is in one stone room at Tallowport to hear the standings read — and the party decides, in public, in front of two hundred masters, what the Sounding becomes. Expose the rot and the compact collapses into open salvage-piracy. Reform it and somebody has to be trusted with the ledger. Take the cartel's place and the party becomes the thing they hunted. All three endings are supported and none of them is the right one.
hook: Ledda has been trying to tell you something for three weeks and you have been getting about a third of it, and on the night after Ambergrace she gives up on tone and does it with objects instead. She lays them out on the cabin table in a line: a rough casting, wet, with weed in the seam. A fragment of crown with half a harbour mark on it. A handful of old moulding sand. And then a small hammered bronze marker of the kind that is set into the reef face at the drop-off, and she puts that one down last and taps it twice and looks at you, and Yevet Ourim, who has been keeping a notebook of tones for a month, says slowly: 'She's saying — I think she's saying, it's all down there. The moulds. The pits. All of it. It's been down there the whole time and they've been using her city to do it.'

articlesAtStake.note: The last honest calling of the campaign comes at the worst possible moment — on the run up to Tallowport with hours to spare before the Hall sits. Answering it may cost the party the session at the Hall. Article One does not have an exception for that.
Somebody may die at Ossary Deep, and if they do they are named and rung out before the ship sails, at sixty fathoms or on the surface, whatever it costs against the clock.

If a hand left at Ambergrace, they are standing on the other side of the Hall at the year's turn, and Article Eight means they are owed nothing and owe nothing. Whether they speak for the party or against them is theirs to decide and the DM should decide it from what actually happened in bw-scenario-003.

acts.title: Act 1: Sixty Fathoms
acts.description: Getting down to Ossary Deep, being received by the quiet folk, and learning what they have been building. This act is exploration and diplomacy, and it hands the party the campaign's largest moral complication before the villain has said a word.
objectives: Solve the descent to sixty fathoms
Be received at the quiet folk's waystation, on their terms
Learn what the quiet folk have been casting for two years, and what it is for

scenes.name: The Bell-Frame at the Drop
scenes.description: The quiet folk's waystation on the reef face, where arrivals announce themselves. Ledda has to argue for the party in front of her own people and there is a real chance she loses.
scenes.readAloud: "The frame is set into the rock at the lip of the drop, eleven fathoms down and four hundred years old: two bronze uprights and a cross-piece with a striker on a lanyard, green with age and perfectly maintained. Ledda takes the striker and hits the cross-piece four times in a pattern and then waits, and the sound goes down the face of the drop-off and keeps going, and you can feel it in your ribs long after you have stopped being able to hear it. Nothing happens for a long time. Then the blue below you stops being empty. Nine of them come up out of it in no particular hurry and stop at a distance that is exactly polite, and the oldest of them strikes twice, and Ledda answers, and then they are talking, and it goes on for a while, and you understand none of it — except that at some point Ledda strikes something short and hard, twice, and everyone stops, and you have very clearly just heard somebody say the word 'no'."

skillChecks.success: You are permitted down. Conditionally, watched, and with an escort, and the condition is stated plainly: whatever you find, you will say out loud, on the surface, in front of your own people. They have watched surface folk find things and go quiet before.
skillChecks.failure: Refused. The party may still get down — the sea is not owned — but they do it unescorted, unwelcome, and without any help at all when the Hollow Bell's working party finds them.

skillChecks.success: A month of Yevet Ourim's notebooks and somebody's willingness to look foolish pays off: a party member answers on the frame, badly, in tone, and the effect on nine deepwater people who have never been addressed in their own speech by a surface creature is considerable. Advantage on the Persuasion check above.
skillChecks.failure: You make a noise on a four-hundred-year-old instrument and it is not a word. Nobody is offended and everybody notices.

skillChecks.success: Ledda is not translating everything. She has said 'no' to something, and it was not about the party being permitted down — it was about something they intend to do afterwards.
skillChecks.failure: A conversation in a language you do not have.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The quiet folk are an original people of this setting: not tritons, not sahuagin, not kuo-toa, not merfolk, and the DM must not describe them or stat them as any of those. They are grey, wide-eyed, bronze-working, and they speak by striking tones. They are also not innocent bystanders — see the next scene — and playing them as noble victims flattens both them and the ending. Their condition on permitting the party down (say out loud, on the surface, what you find) should be honoured in Act 3 and the players should remember agreeing to it.

scenes.name: The Pit at the Far End
scenes.description: What the quiet folk have been casting for two years. The campaign's largest moral complication, delivered without comment.
scenes.readAloud: "They take you the long way round the city, which you assume is caution until you realise it is pride: they want you to see it. Roofed halls, standing doors, streets you can swim down, and everywhere the enormous quiet of a place that has been under sixty fathoms for four hundred years and has not fallen down. And then at the far end, in a casting-pit the size of a barn, there is a bell. Not finished. Not near finished. But even in the mould you can see the size of it, and Anselm Coyle stops dead in the water beside you, because a bell that size is not a harbour bell and it is not a buoy bell and there is nothing on the chain it could be hung in. Ledda strikes two tones, waits, and strikes them again, and Yevet says quietly, 'I think that's — I think she said it twice because I got it wrong the first time. She said it isn't for calling. She said it's for the answer.'"

skillChecks.success: The bell is being cast from the recovered fragments of every stolen harbour bell the quiet folk have salvaged off the Sharrow and the Deep over two years — Nethercombe, Sallow Nook, and four more. It is a monument, and it is also a weapon: hung at the threshold of Ossary Deep and struck, a bell that size would be heard for eighty miles, and it would be heard as a calling with no ship at the end of it, from every direction at once, forever.
skillChecks.failure: A very large bell in a very large pit. You cannot tell what it is for.

skillChecks.success: Ledda is not proud of it. She has argued against it for two years and lost, which is why she came up to the surface in the first place and why she came aboard the party's ship — she is looking for a reason to go home and tell her people to stop.
skillChecks.failure: She is unreadable, as usual, and you assume that is the language.

skillChecks.success: You understand what the quiet folk mean by 'the answer'. If the Sounding is a promise that a rung bell will be answered, then a bell that rings forever and cannot be answered destroys the promise by keeping it impossible. It is not revenge for fifteen ships. It is a proof, delivered in bronze, that the compact was always a lie — and it will work.
skillChecks.failure: Something about an answer. It does not make sense yet.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the scene that makes the ending hard. The quiet folk are not victims waiting to be avenged: they have been building a response, and it is proportionate, and it would end the Sounding for everyone including the Beads hamlets who have nothing else. Do not editorialise. Show the bell, let Ledda be visibly unhappy, and let the players carry it into the confrontation with Corvane Ashe — because Ashe is about to make an argument that this bell half-proves.

acts.title: Act 2: The Moulds and the Ledger
acts.description: The moulding halls, the bronze ledger of ninety-one recast bells, and the master of the Hollow Bell. The campaign's central confrontation, which is an argument first and may or may not become a fight.
objectives: Reach the moulding halls and find the working party
Take the bronze ledger of recast bells
Meet Corvane Ashe and hear her argument
Get out, and up, with the evidence and everyone still alive

scenes.name: The Bronze Ledger
scenes.description: A four-hundred-year-old moulding hall in current use, three casting-pits with the sand freshly worked, and a ledger kept on bronze plates because paper does not survive at sixty fathoms.
scenes.readAloud: "The hall is longer than the Reckoners' Hall at Tallowport and it has its roof on. Racked along both walls, four hundred years deep, are the patterns: every harbour bell on the chain, the originals, still true, with the hamlets' names cut into the wood in a script that has changed twice since. Three of the casting-pits at the near end have been cleared and worked recently. And bolted to the wall at the head of the hall, where a foreman would want it, is the ledger — not paper; nothing is paper down here — but forty bronze plates on a hinge-pin, scribed and hung in order. Sefi gets to it first and turns two plates and says, in a voice that does not sound like hers: 'Captain. There's ninety-one of them.'"

skillChecks.success: Ninety-one recast bells over eleven years, each plate giving date, source harbour, destination buoy and a chop. Forty of them are marked as still hung, which means there are forty false bells ringing on the chain tonight, and the plates say exactly where every one of them is.
skillChecks.failure: Bronze plates covered in a scribed shorthand. You know it is a record and you cannot read it fast enough underwater.

skillChecks.success: The chop on the plates is the chop on the shore-office instruction that sent the Fair Increase, and it is also a Reckoner's chop — the personal seal of a sitting or emeritus member of the Hall. There are eleven people alive entitled to use one.
skillChecks.failure: A mark you have seen before and cannot place.

skillChecks.success: The plates come off the hinge-pin and they weigh a hundred and sixty pounds, and getting them up sixty fathoms is a genuine physical problem that you solve with a lifting bag, a boat's grapnel and a great deal of swearing.
skillChecks.failure: You get eleven plates off the pin before the working party arrives, and eleven is enough for the Hall but not enough for everything.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Let the party understand the scale before the confrontation: forty false bells still hung, tonight, with positions. That is not a mystery any more, it is a rescue problem with a list, and it is what makes the Hall scene in Act 3 actually decidable. Whatever else happens, the party should get at least eleven plates out.
loot: The bronze ledger of Ossary Deep: 40 plates, 160 lb, ninety-one recast bells over eleven years, forty of them still hung with positions given

scenes.name: Corvane Ashe
scenes.description: The master of the Hollow Bell is a seventy-one-year-old Reckoner-Emeritus who sat at the Hall for thirty-one years and wrote most of the modern custom of the Sounding herself. She is not a pirate. She has an argument, and it is a good one, and she has been waiting eleven years to make it to somebody who might understand it.
scenes.readAloud: "She is old, and she is wearing a diving harness of quiet folk make that has clearly been fitted for her, and she is sitting on the rim of the casting-pit with her feet in the moulding sand like somebody waiting for a kettle. She does not run and she does not signal anybody. She says — through a speaking-horn rigged into the harness, so that her voice arrives thin and flat and completely calm — 'Marrach's ship. I wondered which of you it would be.' And then, before anyone can answer: 'You have the plates. Good. Take them up. I mean that. But I want ten minutes first, because in eleven years nobody has come down here who had earned the ten minutes, and you have.'"

skillChecks.success: She means it. She is not stalling, there is no ambush coming, and she is not going to fight the party. She has been alone with this for eleven years and what she wants, more than escape, is to be understood by someone who has answered bells.
skillChecks.failure: An old woman being extremely calm, in a place where nobody should be calm.

skillChecks.success: You place her. Corvane Ashe sat at the Reckoners' Hall for thirty-one years and wrote the greater part of the modern custom — including the nine-mark rule and the breaking-up at the year's turn. Every instrument that has been used against the Widow's Compass all campaign, she drafted.
skillChecks.failure: A Reckoner's chop and an old woman at sixty fathoms.

skillChecks.success: You get the rest of it: the name of every Reckoner on her books, the standing order that keeps the forty bells hung, and the countermand that would take them down. She gives it because you asked her a question she has been asking herself.
skillChecks.failure: She gives you the argument and not the names. The names are in the plates anyway, in chop form, for anyone who can read a seal.

enemies: Corvane Ashe (use a mage stat block, level-appropriate, with water-adapted spells — but she will not initiate combat under any circumstances)
4 thugs (the Hollow Bell's own working party, in quiet folk diving harness)
4 commoners (contracted men from Ambergrace who will not fight and will try to get out of the hall)
2 reef sharks (drawn by the disturbance, arriving on round three and attacking whoever is bleeding)
combatEncounters.tactics: This fight is optional and the scenario is better without it. If the party attacks, Ashe defends herself and her people and tries to break away rather than to kill; the four contracted men flee immediately and should not be treated as combatants; the working party fights competently and surrenders when reduced by half. Underwater combat rules apply throughout: non-piercing melee attacks at disadvantage, ranged weapons other than crossbows and nets limited to five feet, and characters without water breathing on a strict breath count. A dropped character drowns in three rounds. The casting-pits are difficult terrain of deep sand; the pattern racks are cover and will topple; and anyone who cuts a lifting line loses the plates into the pit.
combatEncounters.terrain: A four-hundred-foot stone hall at sixty fathoms, roofed, with three cleared casting-pits, racked wooden patterns four centuries old along both walls, and a single wide doorway to the street. Visibility is good and the light is entirely what the party brought.

scenes.roleplayNotes: GIVE HER THE ARGUMENT IN FULL AND DO NOT UNDERCUT IT. Ashe's case, roughly: the Sounding was never a compact between equals — it is a compact between hulls, and a hamlet without a hull has never been able to call anything in. She spent thirty-one years writing rules to make it fairer and every one of them was ignored by the people with ships. So she took the only instrument the chain respects, which is the ledger, and she used it: the false bells wreck ships whose owners can afford the loss, the salvage goes to Ambergrace, and Ambergrace feeds four thousand people who were starving in the Beads under the Sounding. Fifteen hulls in eleven years against four thousand fed. She has done the arithmetic and she can show her working. And then the party can point at the Charity Bell's forepeak, and at Ryse Halloran's contract, and at Nethercombe's bell in a crate, and she has an answer for each one and the answers get worse as she goes, and somewhere in there she stops sounding like a person who did arithmetic and starts sounding like a person who cannot stop. Do not let her win and do not make her stupid. If the party takes her alive she comes up and speaks at the Hall, which makes Act 3 far better.
loot: The standing order keeping forty bells hung, and the countermand that takes them down
The names of the Reckoners on her books, if the party got them — or the chops in the plates, if not

scenes.name: The Bell of Sallow Nook
scenes.description: Three-quarters finished on the frame in the bell-house: a harbour bell being recast from a hamlet's bell that has not yet been reported stolen. The party can be back at Sallow Nook before the theft is noticed, and what they do about that is the last decision before the surface.
scenes.readAloud: "The bell-house is domed and the acoustics in it are extraordinary and nobody has said a word since they came in. On the frame, three-quarters finished, hanging in a cradle that has held bells since before Tallowport had a quay, is a harbour bell. It is new bronze and it is beautiful work, and scribed on the plate wired to the cradle is the source: SALLOW NOOK. And Anselm Coyle, who has not spoken in an hour, says: 'That's this month's. They haven't even missed it yet. There are people in Sallow Nook tonight who think they have a bell.'"

skillChecks.success: The cradle plate gives the destination too: a buoy station in the Grey Sounding eleven miles north of the Sharrow, on the main route from the Beads to Tallowport, which is the busiest water on the chain.
skillChecks.failure: A bell on a frame with a hamlet's name on it.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Small scene, big function: it makes the ninety-one plates personal again just before the party surfaces. The Sallow Nook bell can be taken up — it is a hundred and forty pounds and the party is already carrying a hundred and sixty pounds of plates, so something has to be left, and that choice is a good one to make them make.
loot: The recast bell of Sallow Nook, 140 lb, if the party chooses it over some of the plates

acts.title: Act 3: The Year's Turn
acts.description: Tallowport, the last day of the year, the Hall in full session, two hundred masters in one stone room, and the party standing up with a hundred and sixty pounds of bronze. The climax is a decision made in public, and there are three endings, all supported.
objectives: Get to Tallowport before the Hall rises — possibly at the cost of answering one last calling
Have the party's own standing read, whatever it is
Produce the ledger in front of the whole chain

scenes.name: One Last Bell
scenes.description: The final Article One test, at the worst possible moment: a calling on the run up to Tallowport with the Hall due to sit at noon.
scenes.readAloud: "You have eleven hours and forty miles and a fair wind, which is comfortable, right up until the moment it isn't. It comes up out of the north-east at about the second hour of the morning watch, thin and far off and unmistakable: three strokes, a pause, two strokes. A calling. Real or false, you cannot possibly know from here, and the last time you heard one in fog you nearly put the ship on the Sharrow. Marda Kell does not say anything at all. Grull Ashpike does — he says it flatly, without pressure, the way he has said it all campaign, because it is a bosun's job to say it: 'Article One.'"

skillChecks.success: You can do both. It is going to be very close and it will cost you the last of the ship's luck, but you can answer that bell and still be at Tallowport before the Hall rises, and the plan you sketch on the chart is the best piece of seamanship anyone aboard has done.
skillChecks.failure: One or the other. That is the honest answer and the DM should give it plainly.

skillChecks.success: The pattern is right for a real vessel: irregular, hand-rung, faltering. Somebody is out there ringing that themselves.
skillChecks.failure: Bronze at four miles. No way to tell.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Do not make this a trick and do not make it free. The calling is real — a Beads fishing smack with a fouled rudder and six aboard — and answering it costs the party the morning at the Hall unless they succeed on the Survival check or think of something better. If they arrive late, the Hall has already read the standings and the Widow's Compass has already been condemned, and the party walks into a room that has finished with them, carrying a hundred and sixty pounds of bronze. That is a better scene, not a worse one, and the DM should be entirely willing to let it happen. If they ignore the bell to make the session, apply Article One as written — a mark, and nobody speaks to them for a day — and let them win their public victory in a silent ship.

scenes.name: The Standings Read
scenes.description: The Hall in full session. Two hundred masters. The brass case open. Every standing on the chain read out, in order, in Avice Holl's carrying voice — and then the party's.
scenes.readAloud: "Two hundred people in a room built for eighty, all of them in wet coats, all of them silent, and the whole chain's year coming down to a woman reading a book aloud. She does it in order and it takes two hours and it is the least dramatic thing you have ever sat through. A mark struck here. Two entered there. A hull condemned — a leeward trader, four marks over, and her master stands up and takes it without a word and sits back down and nobody looks at him. And then: 'Widow's Compass, out of Tallowport.' The room, which has not moved for two hours, moves. 'Standing at the year's turn —' and whatever the number is, you hear two hundred people work out the arithmetic at the same time."

skillChecks.success: The room is not hostile. Half of these masters have lost a hull or a friend on a reef in the last eleven years and every one of them has privately thought there was something wrong with the ledger and said nothing, because saying it out loud is the same as saying the Sounding does not work.
skillChecks.failure: Two hundred people looking at you.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The number matters and the DM should have tracked it honestly all campaign: nine at the start, one struck in bw-scenario-001, and however many the party has worked off by answering callings between scenarios. If they are still marked, the Compass is condemned in this scene, on the table, in front of everyone — and the party then produces the plates anyway, from under a condemnation, which is by far the best version of the ending. Do not fudge the standing to spare them. Let the Articles and the ledger both be exactly as true as they have been all campaign.

scenes.name: A Hundred and Sixty Pounds of Bronze
scenes.description: The party puts the ledger of Ossary Deep on the Reckoners' table in front of the whole chain. What happens next is the campaign's ending and the party chooses it.
scenes.readAloud: "It takes four of you to get it up the Hall and onto the table, and the noise it makes going down is the loudest thing that has happened in this room in a century. Forty bronze plates on a hinge-pin. Avice Holl does not touch it. She looks at it for a long moment and then she reaches under the table and brings up a bundle of her own — two years of notes in her own hand, anomalies she has been quietly collecting and telling nobody about — and sets it down beside the plates, and says, in the same flat carrying voice she reads standings in: 'Then I am not mad. Very well.' She turns the first plate. She reads it aloud. She turns the second. And somewhere around the ninth, a master at the back of the hall stands up and says a hamlet's name out loud, and then sits down, and then it is very hard to hear anything for a while."

skillChecks.success: The room follows the party. Whatever they propose in the next five minutes is what the Bellwater Chain does, and two hundred masters go home and do it.
skillChecks.failure: The room does not follow anybody. It fractures — a third for burning the Hall down, a third for patching it, a third already leaving to go and cut down the bells nearest their own harbours — and the party's ending happens in a chain that has stopped agreeing with itself, which is its own kind of true.

skillChecks.success: You can have this room. It is frightened and angry and it will do what it is told by whoever is holding the plates, and if that is what the party wants, they can have it, and the campaign ends with the third ending.
skillChecks.failure: You over-reach in front of two hundred people who do not take orders, and Avice Holl takes the room back with a sentence.

scenes.roleplayNotes: THREE ENDINGS, ALL SUPPORTED, NONE OF THEM CORRECT. (1) BREAK IT: the party publishes everything, names the Reckoners on Ashe's books, and the Sounding collapses. Two hundred harbours stop trusting the ledger within a month, salvage becomes open competition, and the Beads — who never had hulls and only ever had the compact — are the first to starve. Ledda's people ring their bell. (2) REFORM IT: the party proposes a new custom and somebody has to be trusted with the ledger, and the room will hand it to the party, which is exactly the problem. This ending requires the party to choose a keeper and live with it, and the best version is when they hand it to someone who does not want it — Avice Holl, or Pellamy Doss for whatever weeks he has left. (3) REPLACE IT: the party takes the Hollow Bell's position. They hold the plates, forty bells, the foundry and the leverage over a third of the Reckoners, and they can run the chain better than Ashe did, and they would. Play this straight if they choose it: the campaign ends with the party in Ashe's chair, having done the arithmetic, and Ledda leaving the ship without a word. Whichever they choose, close on the specific consequence for one named place — Nethercombe, Sallow Nook, or the hamlet at Coyne — because that is where the campaign started.
loot: The Widow's Compass, either cleared or condemned, and either way still theirs to sail out of Tallowport

scenes.name: Where Idony's Money Went
scenes.description: The last scene of the campaign. Two minutes, after everything, and the answer to a question the party has been carrying since the first act of the first scenario.
scenes.readAloud: "Afterwards, when the Hall has emptied and the arguing has moved to the taverns, Avice Holl finds you and hands you a fund book without any preamble at all. 'Marrach,' she says. 'Eleven years. Paid in quarterly, never missed, never signed for.' You open it. It is a victualling fund: flour, salt, oil and line, delivered four times a year to three Beads hamlets who lost their harbour bells and could not afford to replace them — Nethercombe, and two others. Every quarter for eleven years, paid out of a master's own share, by a woman who died without a coin to her name and let nine marks stand against her ship rather than explain where the money had gone. Holl closes the book for you. 'She came to me once,' she says. 'Nine years ago. She said the bells were false and I told her to enter a note.' And then, after a moment, the only unprofessional thing anyone has ever heard her say: 'I have thought about that a great deal.'"
scenes.roleplayNotes: End the campaign here, on this, not on the vote. If Ondine Marrach is still aboard — or standing on the other side of the hall after taking Lowther's offer in bw-scenario-003 — this is her scene and it should be handed to her entirely: she has spent the whole campaign not knowing whether her mother was a coward, and this is the answer, and it is better than she hoped and much harder to carry. Ring out Idony Marrach properly on the quay at Tallowport with whatever bell the party has. Then let them sail.
loot: Idony Marrach's fund book: eleven years of quarterly victualling to three Beads hamlets, paid out of a master's own share

npcsInvolved.name: Reckoner-Emeritus Corvane Ashe
npcsInvolved.role: Master of the Hollow Bell / Antagonist
npcsInvolved.description: Seventy-one, small, entirely calm, in a quiet folk diving harness fitted for her. She sat at the Reckoners' Hall for thirty-one years and wrote most of the modern custom of the Sounding herself, including the nine-mark rule that has been used against the party all campaign. She is not a pirate, has never personally rung a false bell, and can show her working. Use a level-appropriate mage stat block if it comes to a fight, which it should not.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Sounding is a compact between hulls and always was, and a hamlet without a hull has never been able to call anything in. She spent thirty-one years trying to fix that with rules and was ignored, so she used the only instrument the chain respects. Fifteen hulls in eleven years against four thousand people fed at Ambergrace. She has done the arithmetic. She cannot stop doing the arithmetic.

npcsInvolved.name: Reckoner Avice Holl
npcsInvolved.role: Harbour Reckoner, Tallowport / Ally at last
npcsInvolved.description: The clerk who read the party's standing out in the first scenario and did not look pleased about striking their first mark. She has spent two years quietly collecting anomalies in the ledger and telling nobody, because saying it out loud is the same as saying the Sounding does not work. She produces her notes the instant somebody else goes first.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The ledger must be true. She has been alone with the suspicion that it is not for two years and it has cost her more than she will ever say.

npcsInvolved.name: Ledda of Ossary
npcsInvolved.description: The campaign's most complicated ally. She came up to the surface because she has argued against her own people's great bell for two years and lost, and she came aboard the party's ship looking for a reason to go home and tell them to stop. Whether she gets one depends entirely on which ending the party chooses. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/ledda-of-ossary.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be able to go home and say: they answered. If the party gives her that, she leaves the ship happy. If they take the third ending, she leaves without a word.

npcsInvolved.name: Pellamy Doss
npcsInvolved.description: He has budgeted his remaining months against the year's turn and this is the day he budgeted for. He swears to the three false entries he wrote, in front of two hundred masters, and names who told him to write them. It is the last useful thing he does and he is entirely calm about that. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/pellamy-doss.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To put right three entries in a book, out loud, in front of everyone, while he still can.

npcsInvolved.name: Ondine Marrach
npcsInvolved.description: The campaign's emotional through-line closes on her. She has spent fourteen scenarios' worth of sessions not knowing whether her mother ignored nine bells out of cowardice, and she found the second ledger months ago and has been sitting on it. The fund book answers it. Full file at data/defaults/bellwater/npcs/ondine-marrach.json.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To find out who her mother was. She gets an answer that is better than she hoped and heavier than she expected.

npcsInvolved.name: Vennor Lowther
npcsInvolved.description: He comes to Tallowport for the year's turn because every insurer does, and he is in the room when the plates go on the table. He does not run, does not deny anything, and says one thing to the party afterwards that they will think about for a long time: 'You have not fed anybody yet.'
npcsInvolved.motivation: To find out what the chain decides, because he will still be doing business in it next year whatever that is.

rewards.gold: Approximately 900 gp in shares — recovered bronze, the Hollow Bell working party's stores and gear, and a purse raised at the Hall by masters who understood immediately what the plates were worth to them. Article Two applies to all of it and the count should be done in front of everyone, one last time.
items: The bronze ledger of Ossary Deep — 40 plates, ninety-one recast bells over eleven years, forty still hung with positions given
Corvane Ashe's Reckoner's chop, and the countermand that takes forty false bells down
The recast harbour bell of Sallow Nook, if the party chose to carry it up
Idony Marrach's fund book: eleven years of quarterly victualling to three Beads hamlets
The Widow's Compass, cleared or condemned, and either way still theirs
rewards.story: The Bellwater Chain knows what was done to it, and what happens next was decided by the party in a stone room in front of two hundred masters. Forty false bells can be taken down tonight because the plates say where every one of them is. Three Beads hamlets find out who has been victualling them for eleven years. And a nineteen-year-old first mate finds out that her mother heard nine bells she knew were false, could not prove it, let the marks stand rather than explain where her money had gone, and died of a fever at Tallowport with nine marks against her name and three hamlets fed.

twists: The quiet folk are not innocent. They have spent two years casting a bell large enough to be heard for eighty miles, from the fragments of every stolen harbour bell they have recovered, and it is not for rescue — it is a proof, delivered in bronze, that the compact was always a lie, and hanging it would end the Sounding for everyone including the hamlets who have nothing else.

The master of the Hollow Bell is a Reckoner-Emeritus who wrote the nine-mark rule herself. Every instrument used against the Widow's Compass all campaign was drafted by the woman at the bottom of it, and she will explain exactly why, with her working shown.

Ashe's arithmetic is not obviously wrong. Fifteen hulls in eleven years against four thousand people fed at Ambergrace who were starving in the Beads under the Sounding. The party has to answer that with the Charity Bell's forepeak and Ryse Halloran's contract, and it is a real argument rather than a rhetorical one.

The last calling of the campaign comes at the worst possible moment and it is real. Answering it may cost the party the session at the Hall, and Article One does not have an exception for that. Arriving late, after the Compass has already been condemned, is the better scene.

Idony Marrach died without a coin because she had been paying quarterly for eleven years into a fund that victualled three Beads hamlets who had lost their bells. She let nine marks stand rather than explain where the money went. Avice Holl has the fund book and has had it all along.
dmTips: THE ENDING IS A DECISION, NOT A FIGHT, and the whole scenario should be built to arrive at that room. There is exactly one optional combat encounter in the entire scenario and the campaign is better if it does not happen. If your table wants a climactic battle, the honest answer is that this is not that campaign, and the Hall scene will be more memorable than any fight you could stage at sixty fathoms.

GIVE CORVANE ASHE HER FULL ARGUMENT AND MEAN IT. Write it out before the session if you need to. She is not mad, not greedy and not a hypocrite; she is a reformer who ran out of legitimate instruments and picked up an illegitimate one, and she has kept doing the arithmetic ever since because the arithmetic is the only thing holding her together. Do not let the party win the argument cheaply and do not let her win it at all.

THE QUIET FOLK'S BELL COMPLICATES EVERYTHING AND THAT IS ITS ONLY JOB. Show it in Act 1, before Ashe speaks, so that when she says the Sounding was always a compact between hulls the party has just seen sixty fathoms of evidence that somebody else agrees with her. Ledda should be visibly unhappy about it throughout and should never explain herself fully.

ALL THREE ENDINGS ARE REAL AND NONE IS CORRECT. Break it and the Beads starve first. Reform it and somebody has to hold the ledger, and the room will try to hand it to the party. Replace it and the party becomes the thing they hunted, competently. Prepare the specific consequences for one named hamlet under each ending — Nethercombe is the obvious choice — and close the campaign on that rather than on a summary.

TRACK THE STANDING HONESTLY AND DO NOT FUDGE IT. Nine at the start, one struck in the first scenario, and however many the party worked off between sessions by answering callings. If they are still marked at the year's turn, the Widow's Compass is condemned in public in Act 3 — and then they put the plates on the table anyway, from under a condemnation, which is the best version of this ending. Let it happen.

UNDERWATER RULES MATTER ALL THROUGH ACTS 1 AND 2. Non-piercing melee at disadvantage, ranged weapons other than crossbows and nets at five feet, movement halved without a swim speed, and a strict breath count for anyone without water breathing. A character dropped to 0 hit points at sixty fathoms drowns in three rounds. Solve the party's breathing problem generously in Act 1 — the quiet folk will help, or a diving bell can be built at Tallowport — and then hold the rules firmly once it is solved.

DO NOT INVENT A SHIP-COMBAT SUBSYSTEM IN THE LAST SCENARIO EITHER. There is no naval battle in this campaign and adding one at the end would betray fourteen sessions of the ship being a home rather than a weapon. If vessels meet, the action happens on the deck where the characters are standing, with the ordinary rules.

PELLAMY DOSS SHOULD SPEAK AT THE HALL AND THEN STOP. He has budgeted his months against this day and it is the last useful thing he does. Play his testimony flatly and briefly — three entries, three dates, and the name of who told him to write them — and let the room's reaction carry it. Do not give him a death scene in this scenario; let him be alive and finished, and let the players decide what to do with the rest of his weeks.

END ON THE FUND BOOK. Not the vote, not the arrest, not the loot. Avice Holl hands over eleven years of quarterly victualling paid out of a dead woman's own share, and says the only unprofessional sentence of her life, and if Ondine Marrach is in the room the scene belongs entirely to her. Then ring Idony Marrach out on the quay and let the party sail.

PACE IT AS FOUR SESSIONS: the descent, the waystation and the great bell; the moulding halls and the ledger; Corvane Ashe; the year's turn at the Hall. Give the Hall a whole session — two hundred people in a stone room and a book being read aloud is a better climax than it sounds, and the players will have been waiting fourteen sessions for that number to be said out loud.
